title: Ushas, the dawn who wakes the world
hookLine: the sky going pale over a parking lot, and a Vedic singer who saw the same light and gave it a name
carry: the vedas still greet every dawn
tomorrow: the ocean is churned, and a healer rises holding a pot.

cards: Early, before the alarm. Out the window, the sky over the parking lot goes from black to gray to something like the inside of a peach. A bird starts, then another.
Nobody will write a hymn about this morning. But weeks of this year went into hymns that did exactly that, sung to the fire, to the storm, to the dark before creation, and to this light.
Today's summit sit climbs back to the Vedas themselves, and to Ushas, the dawn.

teach.h: THE DAWN WAKES EVERY LIVING THING.
teach.b: In the Rig Veda, the dawn is a goddess, and the singers talk to her like someone they know.

In one hymn, in paraphrase, she wakes every living thing and sends each off to its own work: one to look for food, one to its task, one to its prayer. She travels the same path every morning, never wearing out.

teach.h: THOSE BEFORE US, US, THOSE AFTER.
teach.b: The people who watched the dawns before us are gone, the hymn says. We are the ones seeing her now, and others will come after us who will see her too. From up here, look how much of the Vedas stretch was like that.
The very first hymn of the Rig Veda calls on Agni, the fire. Vasishtha asks Varuna why their friendship went cold. A hymn quotes, out loud, the people who doubt Indra exists.
The hymn of creation ends with or perhaps not. The Atharva Veda sits at a sickbed with a glass of water. And the Gayatri turns out to be a verse to Savitr, the sun as the one who sets things moving.
The year found that the Vedas aren't only ancient rules. They are people talking to the world as if it could hear: the fire, the water, the dark and the morning. And they aren't only old.
In many Hindu homes, someone still greets the sunrise the way the singers did, with the morning prayer called sandhya and the Gayatri: may we meditate on the light of Savitr; may it stir our minds.
Ushas arrives every day. The hymn says we are the ones seeing her now.

how: Vedic hymns are recited from memory in traditional schools of chanting, and Hindus who keep a morning practice may greet the day with prayers such as the Gayatri, often facing the rising sun.

games.q: you're a Vedic singer at first light. you've praised the dawn for waking everyone. where does the hymn turn next?
o: to a list of rules for the morning.
to the people who saw dawns before us, and those who will after.
to a warning about sleeping late.
games.why: the hymn turns to time: those before us are gone, we see her now, and others will see her after us.

practice: Look at the light in a window, whatever the hour, or remember the last sunrise you saw.

Bring to mind those who watched dawns before you, a grandparent, someone gone, and those who will see dawns after you, and sit in the middle of that line; if you pray, greet the dawn as the singers did.
If missing someone weighs heavy today, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the Vedas themselves, and Ushas, the dawn who wakes every living thing. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: uṣas, the dawn, a goddess in the Rig Veda.

carryVoice: Your line: the Vedas still greet every dawn. Every dawn has had its watchers; this one has you. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 1.1 (to Agni); 7.86 (Vasishtha to Varuna); 2.12 (Indra and the doubters); 10.129 (creation); 3.62.10 (the Gayatri, to Savitr)
